parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Which company do you work for, and what does an ordinary working day look like for you from start to finish?

I work at one of the drone operating companies. My job as a fleet technician is to keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, which involves adding new drones, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can also ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.
Could you walk me through a typical shift—what do you do first thing when you start, what keeps you busy during the day, and how do you wrap up?
I don't know.
Let's look at the tasks you mentioned—like taking drones out of service, putting them back, or sending them to charge. How do you find out which drones need your attention?
I don't know.
Who hands work over to you, and who do you hand work over to once a drone or charging pad is ready?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?
I don't know.
What do you check by hand today because you do not trust the current tools or information?
I don't know.
What are you most afraid a new software service would get wrong?
I don't know.
When you add a new drone to the fleet or retire an old one, what information do you have to record or deal with?
I don't know.
When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you have to show them?
I don't know.
When you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge, what does that involve for you?

I set up our charging pads at our sites, and I also send drones to charge. We have our own charging pads at our sites, a few dozen of them, which use specific charging connectors that are not interchangeable.
What happens if someone tries to send a drone to a charging pad that doesn't have the right connector, or how do you prevent that?
I don't know.
Besides the connector type, what else differs between your drones or your charging pads?

Our drones are of several models from different manufacturers, differing in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. We also have charging equipment and charging pads at our sites, with several connector types in use that are not interchangeable.
How many drones are in your fleet, and how do you keep track of where each one is and whether it is working or in repair?

We run a few hundred drones and a few dozen charging pads at our sites. I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and I also add new drones and retire old ones. I don't know how to keep track of where each one is.
Is there anything else you can tell me about your sites, your repairs, or how your company works with the platform?

Each company runs its own systems, such as billing and customer updates, that need to hear about what happens to its drones and jobs. Our repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Each of our sites has a few dozen charging pads, and each drone has a home site.
Can a drone charge or be serviced at a site that is not its home site?
I don't know.
